common_name: Royanum Hens and Chicks (Apple-Green Houseleek with Maroon Tips)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the soil surface in a lean, gritty, fast-draining mix in full sun, needing almost no rooting depth to establish.

directions: This naturally occurring alpine form produces large, open rosettes of smooth apple-green leaves tipped in maroon, sometimes showing faint wavy wax markings across the leaf surface. It multiplies readily by short stolons, filling in troughs, rock crevices, and gravel gardens within a couple of seasons. Like other houseleeks, each rosette is monocarpic and sends up a single tall flowering stalk after several years before dying back, leaving a ring of offsets behind. Give it the same spare, dry treatment as other sempervivums; soggy soil in winter is far more damaging than cold.

common_name: Gold Bug Hens and Chicks (Lime-Yellow Heuffelii with Orange Tips)

planting.note: Divide and transplant rosette clusters in spring into sharply drained, gritty soil in full sun to light shade.

directions: Unlike true sempervivums, this heuffelii cultivar divides at the crown rather than sending out stolons, so clusters slowly thicken into a tight dome of small rosettes instead of spreading chicks on runners. Foliage opens lime to yellow in the leaf centers with orange to red tips, then deepens toward burgundy as temperatures drop in fall and winter. It stays compact and rarely exceeds a few inches across per rosette, making it well suited to trough gardens and crevice plantings. Keep soil on the lean side and avoid standing water, especially through winter dormancy.

common_name: Toronto Hens and Chicks (Symmetrical Wine-Red Heuffelii)

planting.note: Set divided crowns at soil level in gritty, lean soil in full sun; established clumps need very little attention.

directions: This heuffelii selection forms a neat, symmetrical rosette in a solid, deep wine-red that holds its color well through the growing season rather than fading in summer heat. As with other heuffelii types, new rosettes form by crown division rather than stoloniferous chicks, so the plant thickens into a tidy cluster over time. It is very cold tolerant and drought tolerant once established, needing only gritty, sharply drained soil and full sun to keep its tight form and deep color. Separate congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor and share divisions.

common_name: Torrid Zone Hens and Chicks (Glossy Copper-Red Heuffelii)

planting.note: Divide congested crowns in spring and replant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun for best color.

directions: A vigorous heuffelii cultivar with glossy foliage flushed bronze to bright orange-red around a contrasting green center, the leaf margins fringed with fine cilia that catch the light. Rosettes grow larger than many heuffelii selections, forming tidy clumps as the crown divides rather than spreading by stolons. Color intensifies toward purple in cold weather, and short stalks of pale yellow to pink flowers appear in late spring on mature rosettes. It tolerates hard freezes without protection as long as the soil drains quickly, since wet winter soil is a bigger threat than cold.

common_name: Allegra Echeveria (Blue-Gray Rosette with Creamy Yellow Margins)

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets in fast-draining succulent mix in bright light after frost danger passes; bring indoors before freezing weather.

directions: This hybrid forms an open, cupped rosette of powdery blue-gray leaves tinged in mauve, with soft creamy yellow coloring highlighting the upper leaf margins. It is a free offsetting type, gradually building into a mounding cluster of rosettes that looks striking massed in a shallow container. A tall stalk of fuchsia and orange flowers rises above the foliage in summer, attracting pollinators. Keep the farina-coated leaves dry when watering and give it bright light year-round to hold its compact shape and best coloring; protect from frost since this cultivar is not reliably cold hardy.

common_name: Irish Mint Echeveria (Upright Mint-Green Tubular Rosette)

planting.note: Plant offsets in gritty, fast-draining soil in bright light once nights stay reliably above freezing.

directions: A hybrid of Echeveria derenbergii and Echeveria runyonii 'Topsy Turvy', this cultivar carries bright mint-green, upswept tubular leaves rather than the flat rosette typical of most echeverias. It readily produces pups around the base of the mother rosette, which can be separated once rooted to start new plants. Pink-orange flowers appear on arching stems in spring and summer and are attractive to hummingbirds. Provide very porous soil, strong light, and infrequent deep watering, and bring it under cover well before any frost since it has no cold hardiness.
